correctness.rationale: For two available seats, the second greedy step optimizes the exact global PAV score among the two pairs containing the unique first-stage candidate. Therefore a strict global/greedy disagreement requires the global optimum to exclude the unique most-approved candidate. A nonnegative-integer parameterization gives \(n=3a+3d_B+3d_C+4+2u+2v+3z+w\), with \(d_B,d_C\ge1\). The second greedy score difference is \((v-u)/2\), forcing \(u\ne v\) and \(n\ge12\). Equality yields exactly two normalized profiles, six after relabeling. Direct scores prove the explicit witness and universal ballots preserve all strict comparisons for every \(n\ge12\). Standalone independent-rule enumeration of 50,387 anonymous profiles with one to twelve voters reports exactly six strict \(n=12\) witnesses and none smaller; the general theorem follows from algebra, not enumeration.

originality.rationale: The base ten-voter PAV committee-nonmonotonicity example and global/greedy divergence are explicitly prior art (Lackner–Skowron Appendix A Prop A.2 and Example 2.5). Unlike those examples, the final claim isolates the smallest absolutely tie-free disagreement and classifies every anonymous profile at that boundary. Searches of published research and comparison with prior claims did not reveal this twelve-voter six-profile statement. This is provisional best-knowledge originality; broader unexamined classifications remain a priority risk.

value.rationale: A strictly tie-free comparison removes an important ambiguity identified in multiwinner-tie research. The three-candidate/two-seat domain is the smallest nontrivial committee choice; the first permissible number of voters is a natural finite invariant. Unlike a routine example, the finding gives an exact lower bound, a complete equality classification and an all-larger-electorate witness family. The normal-form identity explains the required extra two voters relative to the previously known tied ten-voter example. Applications include transparent test cases for comparing optimization with its greedy approximation.
